title: Your MCP Server is Bad (and you should feel bad) - Jeremiah Lowin, Prefect
talk_summary: Jeremiah Lowin (FastMCP author) argues MCP servers are agent-facing product interfaces, not REST wrappers, and that agents differ from humans on discovery (expensive every handshake), iteration (slow, history resends), and context (tiny). He gives concrete heuristics: outcomes over operations, flatten arguments, instructions-as-context, errors-as-prompts, respect token budget, and curate ruthlessly (50 tools per agent is the degradation point).

takeaways.technique: Outcomes over operations (one tool = one agent story)
takeaways.what_they_do: Instead of exposing atomic API endpoints and letting the agent orchestrate multi-step sequences, they bury the sequence inside one agent-facing tool that returns the outcome.

takeaways.technique: Respect the token budget / curate ruthlessly
takeaways.what_they_do: Treat handshake tool schemas as scarce context; keep tool count per agent low and split/namespace servers rather than dumping everything.
takeaways.evidence_quote: 50 tools to the agent is where you start to see performance degradation
takeaways.numbers: 50 tools per agent threshold; GitHub server ~170-200k tokens on handshake; 800 endpoints leaves ~250 tokens each in a 200k window

takeaways.what_they_do: Every tool error response is read by the LLM as information, so they write helpful, recovery-oriented error messages instead of raw exceptions/codes, sometimes deferring docs into errors to save handshake tokens.
takeaways.evidence_quote: you actually have an opportunity to document your API through errors

takeaways.what_they_do: Replace nested config dicts with top-level primitive args and constrained enums so the agent can't invent invalid structures; avoid tightly coupled args.
takeaways.evidence_quote: Just don't ask your um LLM to invent complex arguments

takeaways.what_they_do: Examples in tool docs strongly constrain output shape (e.g. two tags in example => always two tags), so examples must be chosen deliberately.
takeaways.evidence_quote: if your example has two tags, you will never get 10 tags

takeaways.technique: Don't use the LLM as orchestrator when the algorithm is known
takeaways.what_they_do: Reserve agent orchestration for cases where the algorithm is unknown; encode known sequences in code/tools instead of asking the model to plan them.
takeaways.evidence_quote: agents are right in the middle because they can do it but it's expensive and slow and annoying and hard to debug and stochastic
